You topped off the oil sump, there is no leak anywhere on the machine, and a week later the low oil level alarm is back. With no oil on the ground, that oil never left the system. It migrated, and it heads for the coldest point in the circuit, which on most machines is the evaporator.

This one works through every way that happens when you do not know the model yet: off cycle migration, an oil heater that is not doing its job, an oil recovery circuit that cannot pull the oil back, and differential pressure too low to drive the return. Then the much simpler fix on DX and brazed plate machines, and why a check valve will not stop any of it.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Why a low oil alarm with no leak points to migration, and why the oil heater is the first thing to confirm
- Off cycle migration with working oil heaters, and why the RTHD is especially sensitive to a small trickle of water through an evaporator that is not fully isolated
- How an overfed eductor loads the sump with refrigerant, so the oil rides that refrigerant to the evaporator at shutdown
- Oil recovery circuits on flooded and falling film evaporators: eductors, jet pumps, and the gas pump style setup Trane uses on the RTHD and RTAF
- A plugged filter drier leaving the eductor, starving the return to the sump
- Evaporator refrigerant level running too low or too high, and why either one keeps the eductor from reaching oil that floats on top of the refrigerant
- Setting the eductor valve, and why one closed too far lets oil stack up in the evaporator
- Why you need enough differential pressure between evaporator and condenser to drive oil return, and how condenser water that runs too cold takes it away
- DX shell and tube and brazed plate machines: it comes down to refrigerant velocity, so raise the condenser pressure setpoint or shut off a couple of condenser fans to push head pressure up
- Multi circuit evaporators where the idle circuit loses its oil while the running circuit keeps the evaporator cold, and external oil separators on air cooled machines that often have no heater
- Why a migrated circuit may need to trip on oil a couple of times before enough oil comes back to stay online
- Why a check valve will not stop migration, and the cost and complexity that come with an isolation solenoid valve
- The YVAA suction isolation valve and the refrigerant migration freeze it was added to prevent, a different problem from oil migration
- VI control on Daikin screw compressors and why condenser fans do more for oil return than the volume ratio does

queue.description:
SUBSCRIBE Learn how to tile the right way.
STOP Using the Wrong Thinset Mortar #diy #tiles #mortar #construction Using a thinset for a tile or substrate that it is not designed to be used  for can lead to failures, so it is critical to use a mortar that is suitable for the  type of tile and substrate in your tile installation. Thinset is basically a mixture of sand, and cement and other compounds to facilitate the hydration process. Thinset is the “Glue” that bonds the tile to the surface to which it is applied, and it does this by growing crystals as it dries and cures. The crystals interlock and penetrate into the surface of the tile and the substrate, bonding it all together. The longer the thinset is able to grow crystals the strong the bond and the strength of the thinset. 
So what kind of thinset should be used in any given application? Well there is unmodified thinset, and modified thinset, and other kinds of thinsets, but we are just going to deal with these two types which are the most widely used. Unmodified thinset is a thinset that has no polymers added to it, a modified thinset is a thinset that has either polymers added to the powder during manufacturing, or an unmodified thinset that is mixed with a liquid polymer on the job site just before it is to be used. Modified thinset is the most widely used mortar these days and is recommended for most applications and types of tile. So why is there polymer in the thinset anyway? Well it is there to help the thinset retain moisture so it can grow those crystals we talked about earlier. Many of the substrates that tile is installed on are very porous and thirsty and will absorb the moisture present in the thinset, which in turn will prevent the thinset from gaining strength, the polymers help with this problem by keeping the moisture in the thinset so it can Hydrate (grow crystals) properly. So when you go to the store you will see that not all thinset cost the same, some are more expensive than the others, well you get what you pay for, the cheaper thinsets have less of the needed components, and the more expensive ones have more, so by extension better. Modified thinsets also add an adhesive quality to the bonding mechanism, as well as flexibility, enhancing the strength of the tile assembly. queue.title: EEV Diagnostics & Expansion Devices with Ty Branaman, Roman Baugh, & Bryan Orr
queue.description:
EEV diagnostics can be confusing, especially when a perfectly good valve looks bad on paper. In this HVAC School livestream, host Bryan Orr sits down with Ty Branaman and Roman Baugh for a deep dive into the electronic expansion valve: how it works, what it needs to do its job, and how to prove whether it has actually failed before you replace anything.

Ty starts with the evolution of expansion devices, from the fixed orifice (piston) and automatic expansion valve (AXV) to the TXV and finally the EEV, and explains what each metering device was designed to control. Roman then breaks down the stepper motor inside the valve, the difference between unipolar EEV and bipolar EEV designs, and how PID control logic lets mini split, inverter heat pump, VRF, and refrigeration systems modulate refrigerant flow far more precisely than a spring-operated TXV.

From there, the conversation moves into field troubleshooting: thermistor placement and sensor drift, pressure transducer readings, liquid line quality and subcooling, flash gas, and why there is no position feedback telling the board where the valve actually is. You’ll also hear practical tips on using a power cycle to overdrive valves closed, opening EEVs for nitrogen flow & evacuation, cleaning corrosion off the valve body, and using an EEV magnet or manual driver to test operation.

What We Cover:

Expansion Evolution: What problem is each expansion device family trying to solve?

Mechanical vs. Electronic: How an EEV’s stepper motor and control loop differ from a traditional TXV.

The “False Positive”: Which sensor or setup faults make a perfectly good valve look bad?

Mimicking Valve Failures: How low charge, liquid-line restrictions, flash gas, or lost pressure differentials disguise themselves as EEV issues.

Commanded Position: What step count actually proves, and what it doesn’t.

Pre-Replacement Protocol: Repeatable tests to run before condemning a valve, sensor, or board.

Live Q&A: Triaging real-world diagnostic scenarios from the audience.

Whether you’re chasing high superheat with a wide-open command, a suspected liquid line restriction, or a step count that doesn’t match what the system is doing, this HVAC troubleshooting session gives you a process to work from outside the valve in before reaching for a replacement. It’s useful HVAC training for anyone servicing modern inverter equipment.

draft.summary: A double-trapped condensate line and a safety shutoff that only covered one system: that’s how a small install detail turned into a costly callback.

queue.title: Double-Trapped Drain and a Float Switch Mistake: Think Physics First
queue.description:
A double-trapped condensate line and a safety shutoff that only covered one system: that’s how a small install detail turned into a costly callback.

In this Short, we walk through a real field miss on a complex, two-system install. Something under the unit shifted and created a double trap in the drain line, and because the float switch wasn’t wired to cut off both systems, one kept running. The fix was wiring the systems in series so a single switch shuts everything down, something that could have been done at install by running a control wire from the closet through the attic.

Nobody got in trouble over this mistake, but pain is an excellent teacher, and the goal is to learn the lesson without the pain. When an install is new or unusual, slow down and think through the physics: how will the water flow, and how is everything wired together? Physics works the same in an air handler, a condenser, or a condensate line.

The best way to be sure is to check one more time. Make that last check your first priority before you leave the job.

#Condensate #FloatSwitch #HVACTips

queue.title: Turbocor Bearing Faults: Why Good Compressors Get Condemned
queue.description:
The Turbocor keeps throwing bearing faults and the inverter tests good electrically, so the shaft gets the blame. Call it a demag and you are replacing the whole compressor. I have made that call more than once, and in hindsight those were probably inverter problems.

A disruption from the IGBTs in the inverter can leave the magnetic bearings struggling to keep the shaft centered. This one walks through the order I wish I had followed: change the inverter first, see if the bearing faults improve, and only then condemn the compressor for a demagnetized shaft. It also covers how to lay that choice out for the customer up front, and why the inverter is not a wasted expense even if it turns out to be the shaft.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Why the inverter is an early suspect for bearing faults: IGBT trouble makes it hard for the bearings to keep the shaft centered
- Why condemning a Turbocor for a demag means replacing the whole compressor
- How the inverter inside the compressor can test good electrically and still be behind the faults
- The Turbocors I condemned for a demag that, in hindsight, probably had an inverter problem
- Changing the inverter first and watching whether the bearing faults improve
- When the faults do not improve, why the demag shaft becomes the likely call and the compressor comes next
- Laying out the choice for the customer up front: a brand new compressor, or an inverter first to try to save this one
- If the inverter does not fix it, why the old compressor still has value for salvage parts
- Why the inverter you put in is not a wasted expense: stored properly, the customer can keep it and use it later

More chiller training: https://chilleracademy.com

queue.title: Good SCR vs Weak SCR: What the Diode Test Actually Shows
queue.description:
The chiller keeps throwing intermittent start failures, you diode test the SCRs, and the readings land inside the factory range. Technically in spec is not the same as good. A reading sitting near either edge of that range, with intermittent faults on top of it, likely means the set is getting weak.

This one runs a diode test on an SCR in both lead directions, shows what a passing part reads, and covers what a pass does not prove. A shorted SCR can blow apart the moment power goes back on, which is why this test comes first after blown fuses or a tripped breaker.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Why SCR testing calls for a meter with a diode test function, which not every meter has, and why diode mode beats checking on ohms
- The test itself: black lead on terminal 1, red lead on 2 and then 3, then swap the leads and run both pairs again
- What a passing SCR read here: OL both ways from 1 to 2, and 0.38 VDC one way with OL the other from 1 to 3
- Where most factory recommendations land: 0.3 to 0.4 VDC
- The tighter 0.36 to 0.38 window that comes from an electronics background, why readings closer to 0.3 or 0.4 get more concerning, and why that is a warning sign, not a number to condemn on
- When a 0.32 reading with intermittent start failures, DC bus alarms, or current faults at startup is reason to change the SCRs out, even though they are still in spec
- Why some SCRs show a reading in one direction on both terminal pairs, and why the other SCRs in the drive become your reference when you have no manufacturer data like Turbocor's
- Why two SCRs failing together is common, all three at once is not, and why the whole set gets replaced even when some still test good
- What a passing diode test actually proves, and why an SCR that reads good can still give you problems under load
- Testing before you restore power after blown fuses or a tripped breaker, because a shorted SCR does not just fail, it can blow apart
- Why SCRs are starting to get phased out for IGBTs, which now handle AC to DC on the rectifier side, not just DC to AC on the inverter side
- Why IGBTs give cleaner power than SCRs, and how harmonic filters clean up both the incoming feed and the harmonics an SCR drive sends back into the grid

queue.title: SCR Testing: The Floating Nut Mistake Most Techs Make
queue.description:
You put your meter lead on an SCR terminal and get nothing. Inside that terminal is a small nut that floats free, and it is not connected to the terminal plate. Probe the nut, or probe a screw that is backed out and not touching the plate, and the meter never sees the SCR. The plate is the connection point, and IGBTs have the same setup.

Then I get into how this silicon controlled rectifier gives a drive its DC bus: AC line voltage in, DC out, and two small pins that carry the trigger signal. You will also see why a contactor has contacts and moving parts and an SCR has neither, and why every SCR is mounted to a heat sink.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- The SCR terminal layout: line voltage in on terminal 1, DC out on terminals 2 and 3, one positive and one negative
- The small nut that floats inside each terminal, same idea as the floating lugs in some scroll compressor terminal boxes
- Why the terminal plate, not the nut, is the real connection point for your reading
- The two mistakes I see techs make all the time: probing the inner nut, or probing a screw that is backed out and not touching the plate
- IGBTs use the same setup: the top plate is the connection point, and the threaded nut underneath is only there to hold the screw and terminal in place
- How the two circuits inside an SCR module turn AC line voltage into positive and negative DC, which is how a drive gets its DC bus
- Terminals 4 and 5, the two small pins a trigger board or SCR control module uses to trigger the SCR
- How a contactor switches, with contact pads you can replace and mechanical motion every time it pulls in
- Why an SCR has no contacts and no moving parts: triggering the gate is what lets current through the silicon
- Why every SCR is mounted to a heat sink, air cooled or fluid cooled, in a soft starter or a drive
- How the amount of heat decides the size of the heat sink and how much cooling it needs
